For a planet on a circular orbit the a-priori geometric probability that it will transit is  

 P(transit) ≃ (R★ + Rp)/a ≃ R★ / a ,

since Rp ≪ R★.  
Because both host stars have the same radius, the ratio of the two probabilities is determined only by the two semi-major axes.

From Kepler’s third law  

 a³ = G M★ P² / 4π²  ⇒  a ∝ M★^{1/3} P^{2/3} .

Hence  

 P(transit) ∝ 1/a ∝ M★^{-1/3} P^{-2/3} .

Let  
 M1 = 2 M2  (star of Planet_1 twice as massive)  
 P1 = P2 / 3  (Planet_1’s period three times shorter)

Then

 P₁ / P₂  = (M1/M2)^{-1/3} (P1/P2)^{-2/3}  
     = 2^{-1/3} (1/3)^{-2/3}

Evaluate each factor:

 2^{-1/3} ≃ 1 / 2^{1/3} ≃ 1 / 1.26 ≃ 0.794  
 (1/3)^{-2/3} = 3^{2/3} ≃ 2.08

Multiplying: 0.794 × 2.08 ≃ 1.65.

Thus Planet_1’s chance of transiting is about 1.6–1.7 times higher than Planet_2’s.  
Therefore the team should preferentially observe Planet_1.

Answer: D
